p.src: Haraguchi's painting was finished. The Tanseikai hung it in the central position of one of the rooms. Then they placed a long bench in front of it. It was there for people to rest. It was also there for people to view the painting. It allowed them to rest and appreciate the work at the same time. In this way, the Tanseikai provided a convenience for the many visitors circulating around this great work. It was special treatment. Some said it was because the painting was exceptionally fine. Others said it was because the subject attracted attention. A few said it was because he had painted that woman. One or two members protested that it was simply because the painting was so large. Large it certainly was. Once fitted with a gold frame more than five sun wide, it looked so much larger as to seem a different painting. Haraguchi stopped by on the day before the exhibition opened to inspect it. He sat down on the bench and gazed at it for a long time with a pipe between his lips. Presently he rose abruptly and made a careful circuit of the gallery. Then he returned to the same bench and leisurely smoked a second pipe. From the very day the exhibition opened, crowds thronged before Woman of the Forest. The bench installed with such care became a useless encumbrance. Only tired visitors sat there to rest, turning their backs on the painting. Even so, some discussed Woman of the Forest as they rested. Mineko came on the second day, accompanied by her husband. Haraguchi showed them around. When they reached Woman of the Forest, Haraguchi looked at the pair and asked, “Well?” “Splendid,” said the husband, fixing an intent gaze on the painting through his spectacles. “The pose, standing there with this fan raised, is excellent. A professional really does see things differently. It was clever of you to notice this. The way the light falls on the face is masterly. The division between shadow and light is sharply defined—even the face alone has extraordinarily interesting variations.” “No, all of that was the model's own preference. I deserve no credit.” “I am much obliged,” Mineko said in thanks.

p.src: On hearing that the achievement belonged to his wife, the husband looked delighted. Of the three, it was the husband who expressed his thanks most formally. On the afternoon of the first Saturday after the exhibition opened, a large party came together. —Professor Hirota, Nonomiya, Yojirō, and Sanshirō. Leaving everything else until later, the four went first into the room containing Woman of the Forest. “There it is, there it is,” said Yojirō. A great many people were clustered around it. Sanshirō hesitated briefly at the entrance. Nonomiya went in with an air of detachment. Sanshirō merely peered at the painting over the crowd, then withdrew. He waited for the others beside the bench. “He has painted a tremendously large thing,” said Yojirō. “I hear he intends to have Sasaki buy it,” said Professor Hirota. Yojirō began, “Rather than me—” but then looked over and saw Sanshirō leaning against the bench with a troubled expression. Yojirō fell silent. “His handling of color is remarkably stylish. It is a chic painting, if anything,” Nonomiya observed. “It is almost too clever. No wonder he confesses that he cannot paint pictures that go pon-pon like the beat of a hand drum,” Professor Hirota remarked. “What do you mean by a picture that goes pon-pon?” “A picture as artlessly comical as the beat of a hand drum.” The two men laughed. The two of them discussed nothing but technique. Yojirō raised an objection. “Once you paint Miss Satomi, no matter who paints her, it could never look artlessly comic.” Nonomiya put a hand into his inside pocket and searched for a pencil with which to mark the catalogue. Instead of a pencil, he pulled out a letterpress-printed postcard. On inspection, it proved to be an invitation to Mineko's wedding reception. The reception had long since taken place. Nonomiya had attended with Professor Hirota, both dressed in frock coats. On the day Sanshirō returned to Tokyo, he had seen this invitation lying on the desk in his lodgings.

p.src: Nonomiya tore the invitation to pieces and threw them on the floor. Presently he joined the professor in commenting on the other paintings. Only Yojirō came over to Sanshirō. “What do you think of Woman of the Forest?” “Woman of the Forest is a bad title.” “Then what should it be called?” Sanshirō gave no answer. He merely repeated under his breath, “Stray sheep, stray sheep.”
